document.description: BC_1526 (Lit) is a four-pass membrane lipoprotein intramolecular transacylase in Bacillus cereus ATCC14579. It relocates the sn-2 ester-linked acyl chain of an N-terminal diacylglyceryl-cysteine to the cysteine alpha-amino group, producing an N-acyl-S-monoacylglyceryl lyso-lipoprotein without adding another acyl chain. The reaction occurs at the extracytoplasmic membrane interface. Target protein chemistry and native lipoprotein product analysis establish this maturation activity; a histidine-dependent acid-base mechanism is supported by structural and functional studies.

document.description: Lnb (BF9343_0945) is a lipoprotein N-acyltransferase of Bacteroides fragilis NCTC 9343. It promotes addition of an acyl group to the free alpha-amino group of the lipidated N-terminal cysteine of an apolipoprotein, producing the mature triacylated form. The protein has an Lnb N-terminal domain and a predicted multipass membrane domain and is structurally distinct from canonical Lnt. The physiological acyl donor and detailed catalytic mechanism remain unresolved.

document.description: lspA encodes type II signal peptidase (SPase II, lipoprotein signal peptidase) of Bacillus subtilis, a polytopic cytoplasmic-membrane aspartic protease of the peptidase A8 family that removes the signal peptide from diacylglyceryl-modified prolipoproteins immediately upstream of the lipidated lipobox cysteine, the second step of lipoprotein maturation after Lgt. Asp-102 and Asp-129 are the proposed catalytic residues. The B. subtilis enzyme complements an E. coli lsp mutant, but unlike its E. coli counterpart it is not essential for viability; lspA-null cells grow, although they are impaired at low and high temperatures, accumulate lipid-modified PrsA precursor and secrete alpha-amylase poorly. B. subtilis lacks the canonical Lnt route but can further N-acetylate lipoproteins through LhaT/YpjA; the LspA-generated product is therefore an intermediate rather than proof of a universally unmodified mature amino terminus.

document.description: YpjA, also called LhaT, is an integral plasma-membrane lipoprotein N-acetyltransferase in Bacillus subtilis. It transfers an acetyl group from an acetylated heptaprenylglyceryl lipid carrier to the free N-terminal cysteine amino group of mature diacylglyceryl lipoproteins on the extracytoplasmic membrane surface. The acetylated lipid is supplied by PcrB-dependent ether-lipid synthesis and YvoF-mediated O-acetylation. LhaT uses the lipid acetyl donor rather than acetyl-CoA directly; the transport mechanism supplying the external carrier pool remains unknown.

UniProt lists three predicted segments whereas the study predicts six helices; exact helix count is not needed to support plasma membrane.

module.title: Bacterial lipoprotein maturation
module.description: Bacterial lipoprotein maturation begins with Lgt transfer of a diacylglyceryl group to a lipobox cysteine and LspA removal of the signal peptide. The resulting diacylglyceryl lipoprotein may remain unmodified at its amino terminus or undergo lineage- and substrate-dependent tailoring: Lnt, Lnb or a compatible LnsAB complex adds a third long acyl chain; Lit relocates an existing chain to form a two-chain lyso-lipoprotein; LhaT transfers a lipid-carried acetyl group. These are distinct product routes, not interchangeable definitions of maturation. The bacterial occurrence envelope includes exemplars from Pseudomonadota, Bacillota and Bacteroidota; it does not assert universal enzyme presence or essentiality. Precursor export, lipid-donor synthesis, Lol trafficking and client functions are outside the boundary.

module.notes: The required core is Lgt followed by LspA. Optional terminal routes describe capacity for a specified product; absence of one route does not negate the shared core, and presence of one does not establish the others. Multiple routes may occur across a repertoire without asserting that they act sequentially on the same substrate. Taxonomy and family membership guide investigation but do not prove activity, compatible complex assembly, donor identity or essentiality. LnsAB requires a functional A/B pair; the S. aureus pair is the explicit module exemplar. S. epidermidis pairing controls are documented separately with verified RefSeq/UniParc identities because the corresponding UniProt records are deleted. No PANTHER ancestor is invented for Lnb, LnsAB or Lit. LhaT carrier synthesis is the separate bacterial_heptaprenylglyceryl_ether_lipid module; the uncharacterized transmembrane carrier-supply mechanism is not filled with a guessed enzyme. LspA uses the current signal peptidase activity GO:0009003; its aspartic mechanism remains supported in gene/family reviews. Primary evidence corrects older review assumptions about Lnt universality and unknown monoderm N-modification. Computational scope: the generic Boolean compiler treats the LnsAB complex annoton as one activity atom and does not itself descend active_units. Family- and member-aware capacity analysis must additionally enforce both compatible partners, product chemistry and donor availability; a bare GO:0016747 match is insufficient. Panel scope: ECOLI and PSEPK have reviewed Lgt/LspA/Lnt panels, and BACSU has reviewed Lgt/LspA/LhaT. Bacteroides, S. aureus and B. cereus terminal exemplars characterize those reactions without constituting complete native upstream gene panels; B. fragilis rescue in E. coli is an engineered context.
